# Persistence

<!-- Generated by `npm run train` from the sources each rule cites. To change a rule for good, change its source or say so in training/feedback.md; the next training run regenerates this file. -->

- **Change a shared stored record by compare-and-swap on the version that was read. Use a read-modify-write update function that the store applies to the record as stored and applies again after a lost race. Never write back a value computed from an earlier read.** A value computed from a stale read overwrites any write that landed in between, for example dropping an item that a concurrent request added. *Check:* Look for code that reads a record, changes or rebuilds its payload, and then writes it back through a plain update or save. Also look for update logic that runs outside the retrying update function. <sub>Identity ADR-1222; Identity csharp.instructions.md; Identity csharp-production.instructions.md</sub>
- **When a save loses an optimistic-concurrency race, retry in a new unit of work that reads the data again. Allow a bounded number of attempts (three in total), then let the last concurrency exception propagate. Never resubmit the same entity without re-reading it, retry without a bound, or swallow the final failure.** Resubmitting the same write overwrites the winner's change or fails again. Unbounded retries can livelock, and swallowing the failure hides it from the caller. *Check:* Look at catch blocks for concurrency exceptions. Check for a fixed attempt limit, a fresh read on each attempt, and a rethrow after the last attempt. *Note:* Retry operations whose outcome doesn't depend on what the caller read, such as revocations, instead of answering 412 Precondition Failed. Operations that depend on the caller's read, such as an If-Match update, answer 412. <sub>Identity ADR-1012; Identity ADR-1020; Identity ADR-1216; Identity ADR-1217; Identity ADR-1222; Identity csharp.instructions.md; Identity csharp-production.instructions.md</sub>
- **Don't change rows whose concurrency token a SaveChanges interceptor manages with set-based `ExecuteUpdate`/`ExecuteDelete` (sync or async) or raw bulk SQL. Load the matching rows, change or remove them through the change tracker, and save them in the unit of work. Stage bulk work in bounded batches.** Set-based statements bypass the change tracker and the interceptor, so the token isn't bumped, concurrent writers and other replicas don't detect the change, and the EF InMemory provider doesn't support them. *Check:* Look for `ExecuteUpdate`, `ExecuteUpdateAsync`, `ExecuteDelete`, `ExecuteDeleteAsync` or raw UPDATE/DELETE SQL in stores, including bulk revoke and prune paths. Check that shared mutable rows carry a concurrency token. <sub>Identity ADR-1012; Identity ADR-1020; Identity ADR-1199; Identity ADR-1217; Identity ADR-1218; Identity ADR-1222; Identity csharp-production.instructions.md</sub>
- **Stage writes that must succeed or fail together on one unit of work and save them once: an entity with the rows it requires (for example a resource and its owner assignment), every part of a multi-part provisioning operation, or the spend of a single-use record together with its successor.** Separate saves let a crash, a refused validation or a concurrent request leave a partial result, such as a record that has no owner or a parent saved without its children. *Check:* Look for several SaveChanges calls or transactions in one operation whose writes depend on each other, or for earlier saves that are kept after a later step fails. *Note:* Don't report per-step saves when the governing decision record accepts them and explains that a rerun converges a write that stopped part way. Read the ADR before reporting. <sub>NCodeGroup maintainer: principal-engineer-review; Identity ADR-1057; Identity ADR-1216; Identity ADR-1417; Identity ADR-1512; Identity outcomes of #592</sub>
- **A store method, or a helper called inside an existing unit of work, stages its changes on the caller's store manager or unit of work. It never calls SaveChanges itself and never opens its own store manager or DbContext. Only the unit-of-work owner commits.** A store or helper that commits on its own splits one logical operation across transactions, leaves precondition reads outside the transaction and costs an extra connection. *Check:* Look for SaveChanges/SaveChangesAsync calls inside individual store methods or helpers, and for helpers or seed contributors that create a new store manager or DbContext while the caller already holds one. <sub>Identity ADR-1012; Identity ADR-1166; Identity outcomes of #827</sub>
- **Make a single-use or one-time operation mark itself used in the same save as its effect, and guard that save with an optimistic-concurrency token so that a concurrent second attempt fails. For a conditional spend, use a revoke or consume that reports whether the record was still active, never one that silently succeeds when the record is already spent.** A 'used' mark in a separate save, or a spend that doesn't fail when the record is already spent, lets a crash or a race run the operation twice and hides reuse. *Check:* Look for completion flags written in a separate save, single-use rows updated without a checked concurrency token, and spend or revoke results that don't show whether the record was active. <sub>Identity ADR-1512; Identity ADR-1216</sub>
- **In consume-once operations, confirm that the stored payload can be read (unprotected and deserialized) before you mark the record consumed or delete it.** An unreadable record must count as absent and must not change state. *Check:* Look for consume or redeem paths that set a consumed flag or delete the row before they decrypt or validate the payload. <sub>Identity ADR-1235</sub>
- **Keep any state that decides correctness or gates a one-time or cross-replica operation in the shared database or shared store. Keep it out of process memory and the local file system. In-memory caches hold only data that can be rebuilt.** Replicas share only the database, so state held in memory or on local disk lets replicas disagree and lets an operation run more than once. *Check:* Look for static fields, singletons, in-memory caches or local files that hold authoritative state or gate setup or initialization in a host that can run as several instances. <sub>Identity ADR-1512; Identity csharp.instructions.md</sub>
- **Publish audit events, domain events and other side effects of a persisted change only after the unit of work that makes the change has committed, through a run-after-commit hook. Deliver an effect that must survive a crash, such as a message, webhook or notification, through an outbox row written in the same transaction and delivered at least once by a background worker with back-off to an idempotent handler.** A rollback or lost race discards the change but not an event that was already sent, and a send made directly after the commit is lost if the process crashes. *Check:* Look for event publishing, audit calls or external sends made before SaveChanges/commit or inside the transaction, and for must-happen effects sent directly after the commit with no outbox. <sub>Identity ADR-1404; Identity docs/audit-records.md; Identity ADR-1166; Identity csharp.instructions.md</sub>
- **Coordinate external resources with commits. Make expensive or external calls, such as a KMS wrap or key creation, before the window between dependent database writes. If the store write fails afterwards, including on a lost concurrency race, destroy what you created before the failure propagates. Destroy external resources that removed records referenced only after the removal has committed.** An external call inside the write window widens it. A failed write without compensation leaves orphans, and destroying before the commit loses resources that are still referenced if the transaction rolls back. *Check:* Look for external crypto or network calls placed between two writes that belong together, remote creation followed by a save with no compensating destroy on failure, and remote deletion inside the transaction. <sub>Identity ADR-1407; Identity ADR-1471; Identity ADR-1476</sub>
- **A sweep for orphaned external resources lists the provider's resources before it reads the stored references, and destroys only resources created at or before now minus a grace period.** Listing first means a resource recorded during the pass is never swept, and the grace period protects resources whose creation is still in flight. *Check:* In sweep or garbage-collection code, check the order of the remote listing and the stored-reference read, and check that a creation-time cutoff is applied before destroying anything. <sub>Identity ADR-1478</sub>
- **When a store deletes an owning entity, remove every dependent row it owns through the change tracker in the same unit of work. Keep foreign keys `DeleteBehavior.Restrict` instead of configuring cascade deletes. Answer `409 Conflict` while the owner still holds records that belong to another party, never a foreign-key violation surfaced as 500.** A partial delete leaves orphans. SQL Server refuses multiple cascade paths, the InMemory provider cascades only tracked rows, and some dependents reference their owner only by identifier. *Check:* Look for remove methods that delete the parent but not its dependents, or that delete them in separate saves. Also look for `OnDelete(DeleteBehavior.Cascade)`/`ClientCascade`, migrations that add ON DELETE CASCADE, and delete handlers that let foreign-key exceptions bubble up. *Note:* Include authorization state such as role assignments held by a deleted principal, in every tenant where it can hold them. Leftover assignments would keep granting authority to a principal that no longer exists. <sub>Identity ADR-1212; Identity ADR-1192; Identity ADR-1466; Identity csharp.instructions.md; Identity csharp-production.instructions.md</sub>
- **An endpoint or handler that deletes an entity calls the store's remove method and relies on the store to remove the dependents. It doesn't delete dependent records separately itself.** Removing dependents is the store's job in one unit of work, and duplicating it in the endpoint splits that unit of work. *Check:* Look for endpoint or handler code that deletes dependent records before or after calling the store's remove method. <sub>Identity ADR-1212</sub>
- **When erasing everything a tenant owns, find the tenant-owned entity types from the Entity Framework model (the entities that implement the tenant marker interface), not from a hard-coded list.** Then an entity that another package contributes is erased with its tenant without any change to the store. *Check:* Look for tenant deletion code that lists specific DbSets or entity types instead of iterating over the model's tenant-bound entity types. <sub>Identity ADR-1212</sub>
- **Apply tenant isolation once, as a global query filter that targets every tenant-bound entity by a marker interface. Give each tenant-bound entity a denormalized, indexed tenant-ID column so the filter is a single indexed predicate. Don't depend on each query passing the tenant itself.** Scoping at each call site is correct only while every call site remembers it, and one omission leaks data. A filter applied by interface also scopes new entities automatically. *Check:* Look for new tenant-bound entities that don't implement the marker interface or lack an indexed tenant column, filters that reach the tenant through a join, and queries that add their own tenant predicate instead of relying on the filter. <sub>Identity ADR-1018; Identity ADR-1411</sub>
- **A lookup that bypasses the tenant query filter (`IgnoreQueryFilters()`) and returns a single row must match a value that a unique index guarantees is unique across tenants, or fail closed when more than one row matches. It must never take the first match. Its filtered column needs an index that doesn't lead with the tenant column, unless the query passes the tenant.** With a value that is unique only per tenant, a first-match lookup reads an arbitrary tenant's row. Without a suitable index, every call scans all tenants. *Check:* For each new `IgnoreQueryFilters()` query, look at `FirstOrDefault`/`SingleOrDefault` and compare the predicate columns with the entity's indexes. *Note:* Don't ask for such an index to lead with `TenantId`: an index without the tenant column serves both the cross-tenant query and the tenant-filtered one. <sub>Identity outcomes of #629</sub>
- **Never lowercase or otherwise case-normalize an opaque, case-significant value such as a Base64Url hash, session id or secret identifier. Store, index and match it verbatim. Add a normalized (case-folded) companion column with its own index only for a string whose match should be case-insensitive.** Base64Url is case-significant, so case folding makes distinct values collide and makes lookups miss the stored key. The companion column exists only to make a case-insensitive lookup use an index. *Check:* Look for ToLowerInvariant/ToUpperInvariant, case-insensitive comparisons or Normalized* columns applied to opaque keys. For each new normalized column, confirm that the lookup is meant to be case-insensitive and that the normalized column is indexed and queried. <sub>Identity ADR-1052; Identity ADR-1112</sub>
- **When a value whose comparison is case-sensitive is filtered through a case-folded normalized column, treat the database filter as a widening pre-filter and re-apply the exact ordinal match in memory. Keep exact predicates, such as booleans and membership in a set of ids, entirely in the database.** The normalized column never drops a true match, but values such as OAuth scopes (RFC 6749) and resource indicators (RFC 8707) compare case-sensitively. *Check:* Look for queries on Normalized* columns whose results are used without an exact ordinal comparison, and for exact predicates evaluated in memory. <sub>Identity ADR-1080</sub>
- **Push filtering into the database through an intent-named store method that filters in the query and projects only the columns it needs. Never page through or load a whole set and filter it in memory. Use generic paging such as `GetPageAsync` only for reads that are truly unfiltered.** Fetching everything and filtering afterwards uses no index, transfers rows and child collections only to discard them, and moves secret columns out of the database for nothing. *Check:* Look for callers that page or list a store and then apply `Where` or other filters, and for store reads that return full entities with included collections or secret columns when the caller uses only a few fields. <sub>Identity ADR-1080; Identity csharp.instructions.md; Identity csharp-production.instructions.md; Identity outcomes of #553</sub>
- **Keep store interfaces free of `IQueryable<T>` and `Expression<Func<...>>` parameters or return types. Name each method for what it fetches and let each backend translate it.** Expression parameters tie the contract to one ORM, let the caller shape the SQL, and force a backend that doesn't use EF to interpret expression trees. *Check:* Look for store interface methods that take or return `IQueryable<T>` or `Expression<...>`. <sub>Identity ADR-1080; Identity csharp.instructions.md</sub>
- **Don't issue a database query for each item inside a loop (N+1). Load related data in one query or in bounded batches, and express exclusion against a variable set of rows as one server-side subquery predicate (for example `!db.Set<T>().Any(...)`) instead of adding one `Where` per item.** Queries per item, and SQL that grows with the data, slow every call and can exceed provider parameter limits. *Check:* Look for repository calls or lazy-loaded navigations inside loops, loops that append `.Where(...)` for each element of a loaded list, and lookup lists that are read again on every page. *Note:* Don't report an entity as loaded several times when the callers share one DbContext and the lookup checks `DbSet.Local` before it queries. <sub>NCodeGroup maintainer: principal-engineer-review; Identity outcomes of #599; Identity ADR-1416</sub>
- **Within one request, resolve related data in the store manager or unit of work that is already open for the main read. Don't create a second one from a mapping or projection function.** A second store manager costs every request an extra context, connection and query, and the two reads don't share a unit of work. *Check:* Look for store-manager or DbContext factory calls (such as `CreateAsync`) inside mapping or projection lambdas, or after another store manager has already served the same request. <sub>Identity outcomes of #839</sub>
- **Implement keyset paging over a stable, unique ordering backed by an index whose leading columns match the filter and the sort. Order by the surrogate key, or for time-ordered lists by the timestamp with the unique id as a tie-breaker. Fetch `limit + 1` rows to detect a next page, encode the last key values as an opaque Base64Url cursor, and treat a malformed cursor as the start of the list.** Rows with equal sort values are skipped or repeated across pages without a tie-breaker. An index that doesn't match makes every page sort or scan. A tampered or stale cursor should restart the list, not fail. *Check:* Compare `OrderBy` and the cursor predicate with the entity's indexes. Look for missing tie-breakers, offset paging, a bad cursor that throws or returns 400, and stores that reimplement paging instead of supplying an ordered query to the shared base. *Note:* Don't ask individual stores to clamp `page.Limit` when they page exactly as the shared base does and caller-supplied limits are already bounded at the API edge. <sub>Identity ADR-1014; Identity ADR-1303; Identity ADR-1223; Identity review of #420; Identity outcomes of #553</sub>
- **Don't keyset-paginate over a string column whose sort order depends on the database collation. Page by a key whose ordering the database guarantees to be stable.** When the `> lastValue` comparison and the ORDER BY disagree under the collation, a page boundary skips or repeats a row. *Check:* Look for paged queries that order and seek on text columns such as names or paths. <sub>Identity ADR-1426</sub>
- **Run each page of a long or background walk as its own untracked (`AsNoTracking`) query in its own short unit of work, and continue until the next cursor is null. Never hold one context or transaction open for the whole walk.** This keeps memory and tracked-entity state bounded however large the data set grows. *Check:* Look for loops that reuse one tracked DbContext across all pages, read-only page queries without `AsNoTracking`, or background queries that load every matching row at once. <sub>Identity ADR-1426; Identity ADR-1223</sub>
- **Index every column that a periodic, background or pruning query filters on, including the timestamp columns that prunes filter on, unless the table is documented as small by design.** Without the index, each pass scans a table that grows with use. *Check:* For new scheduled, polling or prune queries, compare the WHERE columns with the indexes in the entity configuration or migration. *Note:* Don't ask for a new index for an unbounded predicate on a rarely run operation, such as a delete, when sibling stores already use the same pattern under a recorded decision. <sub>Identity ADR-1218; Identity outcomes of #572; Identity csharp.instructions.md; Identity outcomes of #585</sub>
- **Store a field that queries filter on, such as a grouping or lineage identifier, as its own indexed column on the record. Don't keep it only inside a serialized JSON payload.** Payload JSON can't be queried or indexed portably. *Check:* Look for new metadata that is filtered on but lives only in the payload, or that has no column and index. <sub>Identity ADR-1217</sub>
- **Give a table that grows with use a configured retention, enforced by a periodic hosted service. The service runs on a `PeriodicTimer` created from the registered `TimeProvider` and removes rows in bounded batches, each in its own unit of work, repeating while a batch comes back full. It logs any failure other than host shutdown and tries again at the next tick, so only the stopping token ends it.** One unbounded delete holds a transaction and change tracker over everything past retention. A transient failure must not stop retention enforcement for the rest of the process lifetime. *Check:* Look for new growing tables without retention, single queries that remove every expired row, use of `Task.Delay` or the system clock instead of `TimeProvider`, and catch blocks that let an exception other than cancellation end the loop. <sub>Identity ADR-1199; Identity ADR-1303; Identity csharp.instructions.md</sub>
- **Give a store method that stages a bounded batch for removal a limit parameter that throws `ArgumentOutOfRangeException` below one. Order the batch by a stable key before `Take(limit)`, remove the rows through the change tracker, and return how many rows were staged.** With a stable order and a returned count, the caller can tell a full batch from the last one and keep every batch bounded. *Check:* In batch-removal store methods, look for the guard (for example `ArgumentOutOfRangeException.ThrowIfLessThan(limit, 1)`), an `OrderBy` before `Take`, and a returned count. <sub>Identity ADR-1218</sub>
- **In a batched prune, treat a batch whose save lost a concurrency race to another replica's prune as a full batch and continue the loop. Don't treat it as a failure or log it as an error.** Every replica prunes without leader election, so concurrent prunes are expected. A lost race means the rows are already gone and more may still be waiting. *Check:* Look at how a prune loop handles the concurrency exception on save: it should continue as if the batch were full. <sub>Identity ADR-1218; Identity ADR-1303</sub>
- **Don't let a retention prune remove a record whose required termination or cleanup step hasn't run yet. Measure retention from the time of that step, not from the record's expiry.** Otherwise a record such as a session could vanish without ever being terminated, which leaves dependent grants active and parties not notified. *Check:* Check that the prune's selection requires the record to be revoked or terminated and measures retention from that time. <sub>Identity ADR-1223</sub>
- **In production code, make writes that a background loop retries idempotent. Record an identity or per-writer checkpoint (such as each replica's last applied batch number) in the same unit of work and skip writes already applied, or insert under a unique key and skip duplicates. Keep a failed batch and write it first on the next flush.** A save can commit and still report failure to its caller, so a blind retry double-counts or duplicates data such as billing counters or audit records. *Check:* Look for retried flushes that add, increment or insert without a checkpoint or unique key saved in the same transaction, failed batches that are discarded, and approaches that only document the overcount. <sub>Identity ADR-1199; Identity ADR-1303; Identity csharp.instructions.md; Identity csharp-production.instructions.md</sub>
- **A bulk rewrite job reads rows in keyset pages and writes each page in one unit of work with every row's concurrency token checked. It isolates failures per value: it logs and counts a failed value, skips a vanished row, retries conflicts a bounded number of times, and continues the pass.** One bad value or one conflicting page must not stop the pass, and filtering on the old state makes retries idempotent. *Check:* Look for batch jobs that load everything at once, stop at the first failed record, skip concurrency checks, or retry without a bound. <sub>Identity ADR-1407</sub>
- **Regenerate row-level optimistic-concurrency tokens in one SaveChangesInterceptor that overrides both `SavingChanges` and `SavingChangesAsync` through one shared implementation. It always assigns a new token to Modified and Deleted entries, and assigns one to Added entries only when the token is empty. Stores don't generate, compare or copy tokens by hand.** An interceptor that overrides only the synchronous method never runs on `SaveChangesAsync`. Handling tokens by hand duplicates the steps in every store, and a new row can't conflict and may carry a token the caller seeded. *Check:* Look for interceptors that override only one of the pair, Added entries whose caller-supplied token is overwritten, and store add or update methods that create new token values (for example a new Guid string) themselves. <sub>Identity ADR-1012; Identity csharp.instructions.md</sub>
- **When an update changes only an entity's child collection, assign the parent row's concurrency token so that EF marks the row Modified and the interceptor regenerates it.** If the parent isn't marked modified, its version doesn't change and a concurrent writer goes undetected. *Check:* Look for updates that only add, remove or change child items without touching the parent's concurrency token. <sub>Identity ADR-1012</sub>
- **Don't mark a slice version column (one that versions only part of a row) as a concurrency token or let the row-token interceptor bump it. Set it only in the operation that changes that slice.** A slice version must change only when its slice changes, so that consumers reload just that slice. *Check:* Look for slice version properties with `[ConcurrencyCheck]` or `IsConcurrencyToken`, slice versions touched by an interceptor, or slice versions set by operations that don't change the slice. <sub>Identity ADR-1012; Identity ADR-1050</sub>
- **After a write whose concurrency token the save pipeline regenerates, return, cache or build an ETag from the row read back after the commit, never from the copy read before the write. An update method doesn't return the new token. A create assigns its token up front and returns it, and a caller that updates reads the entity again or answers 204.** The interceptor assigns the token during the save, after the store method returns. Stale tokens break ETags, revalidation and polls that compare them. *Check:* Look for code that builds an ETag from the DTO an update returned, or that caches or returns an entity read before its update committed, and for create methods that don't assign and return a token. <sub>Identity ADR-1012; Identity ADR-1166</sub>
- **In production code, have a store report a lost optimistic-concurrency race with a store-neutral exception named `StoreConcurrencyException`, never an Entity Framework type, and handle it in one place. A management endpoint lets it propagate to a filter that answers 412.** Callers stay independent of the persistence provider, lost races are answered consistently, and NCodeGroup repositories use the same name for the same type. *Check:* Look for `DbUpdateConcurrencyException` caught or exposed outside the EF store, endpoints that catch the concurrency exception themselves, and store-neutral concurrency exceptions with another name. <sub>Identity csharp.instructions.md; Identity csharp-production.instructions.md; project-template outcomes of #169; Identity ADR-1216</sub>
- **When an operation applies several changes to the same stored record in sequence, build each change from the record as the earlier changes left it, not from the copy that was originally read.** A later change built from the original record writes the earlier change's fields back and silently undoes it. *Check:* Look for apply loops that build updates from a captured snapshot instead of a working copy updated after each change, and for a missing test that combines two changes to one record. <sub>Identity ADR-1404; Identity outcomes of #551</sub>
- **A multi-step write that offers a preview runs every validation and authorization check in a planning phase before its first write, and the preview path writes nothing.** Then an apply fails only on a concurrent write or a fault, and running it again finishes an operation that stopped part way. *Check:* Look for validation, authorization or 403/409 decisions made after some writes in the apply step, and for any persistence call reachable from the preview path. <sub>Identity ADR-1425</sub>
- **When swapping the active row under a filtered unique index, retire the old row in one unit of work and insert the successor in another, with concurrency tokens checked and a compensating re-activation if the insert fails. Don't rely on EF Core ordering the update before the insert in a single SaveChanges.** EF Core doesn't guarantee statement order, so a single unit of work can violate the unique index. *Check:* Look for code that deactivates and inserts rows under a unique 'active' filter in one save, or that has no compensation when the insert fails. <sub>Identity ADR-1407</sub>
- **Let best-effort updates, such as sliding an expiration or touching a last-activity time, tolerate a lost concurrency race: keep the other request's change, or drop the touch after the bounded retries, instead of failing the request. Throttle frequent touches, for example to at most once a minute.** The concurrent change is an acceptable outcome, and writing on every request adds needless contention. *Check:* Look for concurrency exceptions from expiration or activity updates that reach the caller, and for touches written on every request. <sub>Identity ADR-1216; Identity ADR-1220</sub>
- **A write that records what a background pass reconciled against succeeds only while the source row's concurrency token is unchanged since the pass read it.** Otherwise a concurrent write would be marked as reconciled against settings the pass never saw. *Check:* Check that the update for a reconciliation record is conditioned on the token read at the start of the pass. <sub>Identity ADR-1412</sub>
- **A cached object built from a store row carries that row's concurrency token and records the revisions of the entities it was built from. Every change that is announced on a cache-invalidation channel must also change the row token; regenerate the token explicitly when the change doesn't touch the row. Send the announcement from a `finally` block after the local eviction and token bump, so it goes out even when those fail.** Revalidation by token detects only the changes the token records, and other replicas must hear about a change even when the local eviction fails. *Check:* Look for cached objects that drop their source tokens, announcements sent without a token bump, and announcements skipped when an eviction, seed or bump throws. <sub>Identity ADR-1416; Identity ADR-1351</sub>
- **Read current concurrency tokens for revalidation in bounded batches, using one query per batch that filters by identifier in the database.** This keeps the cost to one indexed query per batch of cached rows. *Check:* Look for token reads made one identifier at a time in a loop, loads of the whole table, or unbounded lists of identifiers. <sub>Identity ADR-1416</sub>
- **Code that must see a write it just committed, such as a seed, a preview or a validation, reads the committed record from the store, not a cached copy that a replica refreshes by polling. Don't put a cache or invalidation seam under store reads. Layer any cache on top without changing the store contract.** The polled copy may not be refreshed yet, and correctness must never depend on how fresh a cache is. *Check:* Look for post-write checks that read a polled or cached provider, and for store interfaces that gain cache or invalidation parameters. <sub>Identity ADR-1204; Identity ADR-1080</sub>
- **Make seed handlers idempotent. Run them in the host, never in migrations or the migration worker. A handler checks for existing data before writing and reconciles a record it owns with the current configuration, replacing it and logging when they differ. A seed that can run concurrently on several replicas guards its commit with a concurrency token and retries in a new unit of work.** Seeds run again on every start or cache miss. Add-only seeding never applies changed configuration, and two replicas may seed the same entity at once. *Check:* Look for seed inserts in migrations, seed handlers that insert unconditionally or return early because the id exists, and retries within the same failed DbContext. <sub>Identity ADR-1073; Identity ADR-1166; Identity ADR-1169; Identity outcomes of #606</sub>
- **Write a database migration so the previous release keeps working against the migrated schema: expand only (add tables, nullable or defaulted columns and indexes). Contract (drop, rename, make required, narrow, or add unique, primary-key, check or foreign-key constraints to an existing table) only in a later release, or migrate the existing data explicitly.** Migrations run before a progressive rollout while the previous release still serves traffic, and that release also runs after a rollback. *Check:* In migrations, look for DropColumn, DropTable, RenameColumn, RenameTable, AlterColumn to non-nullable or narrower types, new required columns without defaults, and new unique indexes or constraints on existing tables. *Note:* This applies where the repository has a deployed database and tracks changes. A repository whose conventions say it is pre-release, with nothing shipped, may change its schema outright. <sub>Identity ADR-1134; Identity ADR-1180; Identity docs/hosting-analysis.md; Identity csharp.instructions.md; NCodeGroup maintainer: principal-engineer-review</sub>
- **In a migration review, flag by hand the changes an automated expand-only check can't detect: a column made nullable that the previous release maps as required, a store-type change that keeps the CLR type (such as `text` to `jsonb`), a collation change, a sequence restart, a dropped unique index the previous release relies on, and a new table's restricting foreign key (`Restrict`/`NoAction`) to an existing table.** Each of these changes how the previous release reads, writes or deletes even though its model looks the same. *Check:* Look at `AlterColumn` `nullable:`, `type:`/`oldType:` and `collation:` changes, `RestartSequence`, `DropIndex` on unique indexes, and `AddForeignKey` or `CreateTable` foreign keys that reference existing tables. *Note:* Like the expand-only rule, this applies only where the repository has a deployed database and tracks changes. <sub>Identity ADR-1180</sub>
- **Never apply EF Core migrations or call `EnsureCreated` from a serving host's startup. A dedicated migration worker or job applies them before rollout and exits, and the orchestrator waits for it to complete (`WaitForCompletion`).
